strengths: The paper presents a clean and non-trivial theoretical generalization of prior byte-level lossless reduction work (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies via the novel notion of 'nested tokenization,' with rigorous proofs (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.4) showing the reduction preserves the underlying text distribution exactly.
The paper includes a clear, hand-worked illustrative example (Section 3.2/Appendix B) that makes the abstract recursive formulation concrete and verifiable, aiding reproducibility and understanding.

An efficient approximate algorithm (Algorithm 2) is derived from the naive exponential-cost algorithm via a principled top-K truncation, making the method practically usable at real vocabulary scales.

The application to model ensembling via maximal common vocabulary (MCV) is compelling: experiments across multiple model pairs and benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACP, MMLU-Pro) show that LVR-based ensembling matches or exceeds byte-level ensembling in accuracy while being notably faster, and it avoids the catastrophic failures observed with heuristic baselines (Union, Naive-MCV) under product-of-experts ensembling.

Experiments are reasonably thorough, including both PoE and MoE ensemble variants, multiple vocabulary-reduction depths (1/2/4/8 bytes), and multiple model families (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon), along with inference-speed measurements and reproducibility details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The practical algorithm relies on a top-K heuristic truncation without any theoretical error bound, which is in some tension with the paper's central 'lossless' claim/title; the empirical near-losslessness is not rigorously characterized (e.g., no analysis of how the approximation error scales with K or vocabulary size).

The theory depends on the validity assumption for deterministic tokenizers (e.g., greedy/BPE forward matching); it is not fully discussed how well this generalizes to tokenizers with more complex pre-tokenization rules (regex splitting, special tokens, byte-fallback edge cases) used by some real production models.

Experimental scale is modest (models up to ~7B parameters, and relatively small per-category sampled subsets of 100 questions for MATH/ACP/MMLU-Pro), limiting confidence that trends hold at larger scale or with more comprehensive evaluation.

While several alternative heterogeneous-vocabulary ensembling approaches are discussed in related work (embedding-similarity-based, partial string matching), they are not empirically compared against, only the union-vocabulary and naive-restriction baselines are tested.

The broader motivating applications mentioned in the introduction (speculative decoding, knowledge distillation, inference-time alignment) are not empirically evaluated, so the practical benefit of the framework is only demonstrated for ensembling.

The construction of the maximal common vocabulary/tokenizer (based on inheriting merge rules from one model's BPE tokenizer) is somewhat ad hoc, and its optimality relative to alternative constructions is not analyzed or compared.

strengths: Establishes a clean and general theoretical framework (nested tokenization, relative covering) that strictly generalizes prior byte-level lossless reduction work (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, with rigorous proofs (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2/3.3, Theorem 3.4) provided in the appendix.
Derives a practical, efficient top-K approximate algorithm (Algorithm 2) from the exact but expensive Algorithm 1, with clear complexity reasoning for why the nested loops can be collapsed.
Provides an illustrative worked example (Section 3.2/Appendix B) that concretely demonstrates the mechanics of the method, aiding reproducibility and understanding.

Empirical evaluation is fairly broad: multiple model families (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, Phi, Yi), multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, MMLU-Pro, and translation tasks), both greedy and temperature sampling, PoE and MoE ensembling, and an ablation over the K hyperparameter and its computational overhead.

Meaningful practical contribution: the maximal-common-vocabulary (MCV) ensemble is shown to be both more accurate/stable than heuristic baselines (Union, Naive MCV) and more computationally efficient than byte-level ensembling, addressing a genuine pain point in cross-vocabulary LLM cooperation.

Good honesty about limitations, e.g., explicit discussion that greedy decoding outputs can diverge between the original and reduced models even though the underlying text distributions are identical (Section 5.1, Appendix B).
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution, while a legitimate generalization, is somewhat incremental relative to Phan et al. (2025)/Vieira et al. (2025): the byte-level case is recovered as a special case (Vsub = A), and much of the machinery (minimal/relative covers) directly extends existing constructions.

K-LVR is only approximately lossless in practice; the paper does not provide a formal error bound or theoretical guarantee on the approximation gap introduced by the top-K truncation, relying instead on empirical closeness to the 'Full' baseline.

The construction of the maximal common vocabulary (Eq. 25) is tied specifically to BPE and to designating one tokenizer's merge rules as canonical (T1), introducing an arbitrary asymmetry between ensembled models that is not deeply analyzed; behavior with >2 models or non-BPE tokenizers (e.g., Unigram) is not empirically explored despite being mentioned as possible.

Main paper experiments are limited to a single ensemble pair (Qwen2.5-3B & Falcon3-7B) in the primary table; while more pairs appear in the appendix, the core narrative would benefit from broader main-text coverage, especially with >2 models simultaneously ensembled.

GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, and MMLU-Pro sub-sampling uses only 100 questions per category in several evaluations, which may lead to noisy accuracy estimates and limits statistical confidence in some reported deltas.

No wall-clock/throughput comparison against the naive full-vocabulary single-model baseline is given beyond the byte-level ensemble comparison, making it harder to judge the practical overhead of K-LVR relative to standard (non-ensembled) inference.

Some notational density and the layered lemma structure (Lemma 3.2/3.3, Theorem 3.4) make the paper challenging to follow without careful reading; a higher-level intuition or diagram summarizing the recursive computation earlier in Section 3 could improve accessibility.

strengths: The paper provides a clean and rigorous theoretical generalization of prior byte-level lossless reduction (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, introducing the notion of nested tokenization and relative covering with full proofs.
The application to ensembling via a maximal common vocabulary is well-motivated and addresses a genuine practical bottleneck (byte-level ensembles being slow due to single-byte generation).

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, Phi, Yi) and benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACP, MMLU-Pro, WMT translation), plus ablations on the top-K hyperparameter and PoE vs. MoE ensembling.

The empirical results show that naive heuristic baselines (union vocabulary, naive restriction to MCV) can catastrophically fail in PoE ensembling, while the proposed K-LVR method remains robust, which is a meaningful practical finding.

Illustrative worked example (Fig. 2, Appendix B) helps ground the abstract theory and honestly discusses a subtlety (greedy decoding path divergence) that could otherwise be seen as undermining the 'lossless' claim.
weaknesses: The 'lossless' framing is diluted by the fact that the exact algorithm (Algorithm 1) is computationally infeasible, and all reported results actually use the approximate Algorithm 2 (K-LVR); the true losslessness guarantee is therefore never empirically realized in practice, only approximated to an unknown degree that depends on K.

The core theoretical contribution is an incremental extension of the byte-level reduction theory from Phan et al. (2025)/Vieira et al. (2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies; the mathematical machinery (validity condition, minimal/relative covering, marginalization) is a natural adaptation rather than a conceptually new idea.

The efficiency/accuracy benefit of the headline application (ensemble via maximal common vocabulary) is not clearly established: in Table 2 the 1-byte K-LVR ensemble actually outperforms the MCV-based ensemble on GSM8K and ACP, weakening the core motivating claim that MCV is preferable to byte-level reduction.

Evaluation on MATH, ACP, and MMLU-Pro uses only 100 randomly sampled questions per category, and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported anywhere, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the (often small) differences between methods.

The maximal common vocabulary construction is tied specifically to BPE merges from one of the two tokenizers, which is somewhat ad hoc and may not generalize cleanly to models with heterogeneous tokenization schemes (e.g., BPE vs. Unigram), despite the paper's claim of general applicability.

Although the introduction motivates the framework with knowledge distillation, speculative decoding, and inference-time alignment, the empirical study only tests ensembling, leaving the broader claimed applicability largely unvalidated.

Inference speed comparisons (Table 3, Appendix D.1) are limited to only two model pairs and a single benchmark (GSM8K), providing a fairly narrow basis for the efficiency claims relative to byte-level ensembling.

strengths: Provides a clean and rigorous theoretical generalization of prior byte-level lossless reduction methods (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies via the novel notion of 'nested tokenization,' with full proofs (Theorem 3.1, 3.4) and a clarifying illustrative example.
Derives a principled recursive algorithm (Algorithm 1) and a practical, efficient top-K approximation (Algorithm 2) with reasonable computational complexity analysis.

The application to ensembling models with heterogeneous vocabularies via a 'maximal common vocabulary' is a compelling and practically useful use case, showing that naive baselines (Union, Naive-MCV) can catastrophically fail while K-LVR remains robust across both PoE and MoE ensemble formulations.

Extensive empirical validation across many model families (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, Phi, Yi), multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, MMLU-Pro, WMT translation), and thorough ablations (choice of K, inference speed, vocabulary reduction consistency), which strengthens confidence in the claims.
Demonstrates measurable inference-speed advantages of MCV-based ensembling over byte-level ensembling, directly supporting the paper's efficiency motivation.
weaknesses: The practical algorithm (K-LVR) is only an approximation of the theoretically lossless procedure; no formal bound on approximation error is provided, and losslessness is only verified empirically via accuracy metrics, which may not fully capture distributional fidelity.

The construction of the maximal common vocabulary and its associated tokenizer is somewhat ad hoc (derived asymmetrically from one model's BPE merges, T1), and the paper acknowledges 'some arbitrariness' without deeply exploring alternative constructions or their impact.

Ensemble gains from MCV over simple 1-byte reduction are inconsistent and sometimes slightly worse (e.g., Table 2 MCV underperforms 1-Bytes on GSM8K and ACP; Table 6 MMLU-Pro K-LVR MCV is comparable to or barely better than the best single model), suggesting the practical benefit is efficiency rather than accuracy.

Although the introduction motivates broader applications (speculative decoding, knowledge distillation, inference-time alignment), the empirical evaluation focuses solely on ensembling; these other applications remain unvalidated.
No direct empirical comparison to the concurrent/related Hayase et al. (2025) byte-level sampling method, despite it being cited as closely related work.

The theoretical framework and notation are dense (relative coverings, nested tokenization, multiple lemmas), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for practitioners despite the provided pseudocode.
